steps.say: So 21 is 3 lots of (2 + 5), which is 3 × (2 + 5). Splitting a total into equal groups is factorising: you write the shared 3 outside a bracket. Now swap the counts for \(x\): 6 blue and 15 gold become \(6x + 15\), and the same 3 rows give \(6x + 15 = 3(2x + 5)\). Taking out the common factor is exactly sharing into equal rows.

method_card.title: How to Factorise Algebraic Expressions
method_card.content:
Factorising is the reverse of expanding: write an expression as a product of factors.

Common factor: take the highest common factor of every term outside a bracket. \(6x + 15 = 3(2x + 5)\).

Quadratic \(x^2 + bx + c\): two numbers that multiply to \(c\) and add to \(b\). \(x^2 + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)\).

Difference of two squares: \(a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)\), so \(x^2 - 25 = (x + 5)(x - 5)\). Always factorise fully.
method_card.example:
Factorise \(x^2 - 3x - 10\)

Step 1: Find two numbers that multiply to \(-10\) and add to \(-3\)

Step 2: \(-5 \times 2 = -10\) and \(-5 + 2 = -3\) ✔

Answer: \((x - 5)(x + 2)\)

steps: Difference of two squares: \(a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)\). Square-root each term: \(4x^2 - 25 = (2x + 5)(2x - 5)\).
Always take out a common factor first, then keep going: \(3x^2 - 12 = 3(x^2 - 4) = 3(x + 2)(x - 2)\).
A perfect square has a middle term: \(x^2 - 10x + 25 = (x - 5)^2\). Check the number doubled gives the middle term.
gold.title: Gold: DOTS, squares and factor first

steps: Factorising reverses expanding. For a single bracket, find the highest common factor (HCF) of every term and write it outside.
Divide each term by the HCF to get what goes inside: \(6x + 15 = 3(2x + 5)\) because \(6x ÷ 3 = 2x\) and \(15 ÷ 3 = 5\).
Take out letters too. If every term has an \(x\), the HCF includes \(x\): \(5x^2 + 15x = 5x(x + 3)\). Check by expanding back.
bronze.title: Bronze: common factor

steps: For \(x^2 + bx + c\), find two numbers that multiply to \(c\) and add to \(b\). They become the numbers in the two brackets.
Watch the signs. If \(c\) is positive, both numbers share \(b\)'s sign; if \(c\) is negative, one is positive and one is negative.
Write \((x + p)(x + q)\) with your two numbers, then expand to check the middle term.
silver.title: Silver: quadratic trinomials

gold.hint: Difference of two squares: square-root each term to get 2x and 5.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (2x−5)² gives 4x²−20x+25, which has an extra −20x term. A difference of two squares needs one plus and one minus bracket: (2x+5)(2x−5).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (2x+25)(2x−1) mixes up the square roots. √(4x²)=2x and √25=5, so it is (2x+5)(2x−5).

gold.hint: This is a perfect square: the number is −5, so it is (x − 5) squared.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+5)² gives +10x in the middle, but the expression has −10x. The number is −5: (x−5)².

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−5)(x+5) is x²−25 with no middle term. The −10x here means it is the perfect square (x−5)².

gold.hint: Take out 3 first, then factorise the difference of two squares.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 3(x²−4) is only half done. x²−4 is a difference of two squares, so factorise again: 3(x+2)(x−2).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (3x+6)(x−2) still hides a common factor of 3 inside the first bracket. Take it fully outside: 3(x+2)(x−2).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 3(x−2)² expands to 3x²−12x+12, not 3x²−12. Use one plus and one minus: 3(x+2)(x−2).

gold.hint: Group x²−6x+9 as a perfect square, then use the difference of two squares with y.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−3)²−y² is not finished. It is a difference of two squares, so factorise: (x−3+y)(x−3−y).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−3)(x−3−y) expands wrongly. Group x²−6x+9 as (x−3)², then apply the difference of two squares with y: (x−3+y)(x−3−y).

gold.hint: Take out 2x first, then factorise the difference of two squares.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 2x(x²−9) stops too early. x²−9 is a difference of two squares: 2x(x+3)(x−3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: x(2x²−18) misses part of the common factor. The HCF is 2x, and 2x²−18 factorises further: 2x(x+3)(x−3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 2(x³−9x) still has an x in every bracket term. Take out 2x, then use the difference of two squares: 2x(x+3)(x−3).

bronze.hint: The highest common factor of 3x and 9 is 3.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 9(x+1) expands to 9x+9, not 3x+9. The highest common factor of 3x and 9 is 3: 3(x+3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 3(x+9) expands to 3x+27. After dividing, 9÷3=3, so the bracket is (x+3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: x(3+9) treats x as the common factor, but 9 has no x in it. The common factor is 3: 3(x+3).

bronze.hint: Both terms divide by 4, so take out 4.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 2(4x−6) is not fully factorised: 4x−6 still shares a factor of 2. The full HCF is 4: 4(2x−3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 8(x−4) expands to 8x−32, not 8x−12. 8 does not divide 12, so the HCF is 4: 4(2x−3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 4(2x+3) expands to 8x+12. The −12 keeps its minus sign, so it is 4(2x−3).

bronze.hint: Both terms share a 5 and an x, so the factor is 5x.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 5(x²+3x) still has an x in both bracket terms. The HCF is 5x, not just 5: 5x(x+3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: x(5x+15) still has a factor of 5 inside. The HCF is 5x: 5x(x+3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 5x(x+15) is wrong: 15x÷5x=3, not 15. The bracket is (x+3).

bronze.hint: Both terms share a 3 and a y, so the factor is 3y.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 3(2xy+3y) still has a y in both terms. Take out the full HCF 3y: 3y(2x+3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 6y(x+9) expands to 6xy+54y, not 6xy+9y. The HCF of 6xy and 9y is 3y: 3y(2x+3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: y(6x+9) still has a factor of 3 inside. The HCF is 3y: 3y(2x+3).

bronze.hint: Both terms share an x, so take out x.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 5(x+x) simplifies to 10x, not x²+5x. The common factor is x: x(x+5).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: x²(1+5) simplifies to 6x², not x²+5x. Only one x is common to both terms: x(x+5).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: x(x+5x) has an extra x that should not be there: 5x÷x=5, so the bracket is (x+5).

bronze.hint: Both terms divide by 4 and share an x, so take out 4x.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 4(3x²−2x) still has an x in both terms. The HCF is 4x: 4x(3x−2).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 2x(6x−4) is not fully factorised: 6x−4 shares a factor of 2. The full HCF is 4x: 4x(3x−2).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 4x(3x+2) expands to 12x²+8x. The −8x keeps its minus, so it is 4x(3x−2).

bronze.hint: No middle term and a minus: use the difference of two squares.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: x(x−4) expands to x²−4x, not x²−4. There is no middle term, so use the difference of two squares: (x+2)(x−2).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−4)(x+1) expands to x²−3x−4. x²−4 is a difference of two squares: x²−2²=(x+2)(x−2).

bronze.hint: No middle term and a minus: use the difference of two squares.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: x(x−16) expands to x²−16x, not x²−16. Use the difference of two squares: x²−4²=(x+4)(x−4).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−8)(x+2) expands to x²−6x−16. Here there is no middle term: x²−16=(x+4)(x−4).

silver.hint: Find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+2)(x+6) gives 2+6=8 in the middle, but we need 7. The pair is 3 and 4: (x+3)(x+4).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+6)(x+2) also adds to 8, not 7. Two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7 are 3 and 4.

silver.hint: Find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to −5; both are negative.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+2)(x−3) gives a constant of −6, but we need +6. Both numbers are negative: (x−2)(x−3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+2)(x+3) gives +5x in the middle. We need −5x, so both numbers are negative: (x−2)(x−3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−1)(x−6) adds to −7, not −5. The pair is −2 and −3: (x−2)(x−3).

silver.hint: Find two numbers that multiply to −15 and add to 2.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−5)(x+3) gives −2x in the middle. Swap the signs so the +5 goes with the larger number: (x+5)(x−3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+5)(x+3) gives +15, but we need −15. One number must be negative: (x+5)(x−3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+15)(x−1) multiplies to −15 but adds to +14, not +2. The pair is +5 and −3.

silver.hint: Find two numbers that multiply to −20 and add to −1.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+5)(x−4) gives +x in the middle. We need −x, so the larger number is negative: (x−5)(x+4).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−5)(x−4) gives +20, but we need −20. One number must be positive: (x−5)(x+4).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−10)(x+2) multiplies to −20 but adds to −8, not −1. The pair is −5 and +4.

silver.hint: No middle term: use the difference of two squares with √81 = 9.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−9)² gives −18x in the middle. A difference of two squares has no middle term: (x+9)(x−9).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−81)(x+1) expands to x²−80x−81. 81 is 9², so x²−81=(x+9)(x−9).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+3)(x−27) is not a difference of two squares. √81=9, so x²−81=(x+9)(x−9).

silver.hint: Find two numbers that multiply to −28 and add to 3.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x−7)(x+4) gives −3x in the middle. We need +3x, so the 7 is positive: (x+7)(x−4).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+7)(x+4) gives +28, but we need −28. One number must be negative: (x+7)(x−4).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+14)(x−2) multiplies to −28 but adds to +12, not +3. The pair is +7 and −4.

silver.hint: Take out the common factor 2 first, then factorise the trinomial.

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (2x+4)(x+3) still hides a factor of 2 in the first bracket. Take out the 2 first: 2(x+2)(x+3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: (x+2)(2x+6) still has a factor of 2 in the second bracket. Take out the 2 first: 2(x+2)(x+3).

misconceptions.note: expect = original option index of this distractor
misconceptions.message: 2(x+6)(x+1) expands to 2x²+14x+12, not 2x²+10x+12. After taking out 2, factorise x²+5x+6 as (x+2)(x+3).
